facts.claim: Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park covers about 167,000 ha between Stawell and Horsham, roughly 260 km west of Melbourne; Gariwerd is the Jardwadjali name for the range.
It was listed on the National Heritage List in 2006 for natural beauty and as one of the richest Aboriginal rock art sites in south-eastern Australia; the area holds about 90% of Victoria's rock art.
The ranges are uplifted, tilted sandstone that form the western end of the Great Dividing Range; the highest peak is Mount William (Duwul) at 1,167 m.
Halls Gap is the only town and main access point; the Wonderland area beside it is the most popular for day walks, and the Grampians Peaks Trail is a 164 km, 13-day walk from Mt Zero to Dunkeld.
Known as the 'garden of Victoria', the park has 975 native plant species including more than 75 orchids, about a third of Victoria's flora, and spring wildflowers are an attraction.
Brambuk, the Aboriginal cultural centre at Halls Gap, is owned and managed by Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung people from five communities.

experiences: Walk to lookouts over the ranges
See Aboriginal rock art in Gariwerd
Spot kangaroos, emus and koalas at Halls Gap

tips.title: Check closures after bushfires
tips.detail: The 2024-25 fires burned over 135,000 ha and damaged tracks and camps. Check Parks Victoria for open sites before you go.

tips.title: Walk in winter or spring
tips.detail: Summer in the ranges can be very hot and dry. Winter and spring are the best seasons for walking.

tips.title: Stay at Halls Gap
tips.detail: The only town in the park, with the supermarket, visitor centre and Wonderland walks beside it. Kangaroos graze nearby in late afternoon.

best_months.rationale: Spring wildflowers and good walking weather; winter and spring recommended for walking, summer hot and dry. Autumn also mild.

seasonal_tags: spring wildflowers (Sep-Nov) only; no other recurring crowd pattern sourced

facts.claim: Port Campbell National Park protects about 1,750 ha of limestone coast along the Great Ocean Road, about 190 km south-west of Melbourne, from Peterborough to Princetown; first dedicated in 1964.
The coast has sheer cliffs, offshore stacks, gorges, arches and blowholes, shaped by the Southern Ocean as part of the Shipwreck Coast.
The Twelve Apostles are limestone stacks formed as erosion cut caves, then arches that collapsed; only eight stacks stood when the name was chosen.
The clipper Loch Ard was wrecked at Loch Ard Gorge in 1878 and only two of 54 aboard survived; two pillars are named Tom and Eva for the survivors.
London Arch (formerly London Bridge) lost its shoreward span in 1990, stranding two tourists.

Little penguins can sometimes be seen at dusk near the Twelve Apostles and London Bridge, short-tailed shearwaters return to Mutton Bird Island between October and April, and whales are often spotted during migration.

experiences: See limestone stacks rise from the sea
Watch whales and penguins from the coast
Follow lookouts along the Great Ocean Road

tips.title: Stay in Port Campbell
tips.detail: There is no accommodation or camping in the park, and sleeping in car parks is prohibited. The nearest beds are in Port Campbell or Warrnambool.

tips.title: Don't swim here
tips.detail: The water is cold even in summer and the beaches are unsuitable for swimming or surfing, so enjoy them from the sand.

tips.title: Come at dusk for penguins
tips.detail: Penguins are best seen in summer just after sunset near the Twelve Apostles and London Bridge. Sightings are not guaranteed.

best_months.rationale: Wikivoyage names December-January as the warmer months and best for visiting; penguins best in summer after sunset; Parks authority says spring and summer have the most favourable weather. Whales migrate through in winter-spring (month range not given in fetched page).

seasonal_tags: none sourced with months (shearwaters Oct-Apr per GOCAPA; whale migration months not stated)
